scenes.visual: Portrait pushes in slowly; name and dates appear.

scenes.tts: In an 1894 Berlin lecture mostly spent being careful, the most formidable organic chemist in Germany let one metaphor escape: to explain why an enzyme would tear apart one molecule and ignore its near-twin, enzyme and substrate had to fit "like lock and key."
scenes.visual: 1894 Berlin lecture; lock and key schematic fit; near-twin ignored
scenes.narration: In an 1894 Berlin lecture mostly spent being careful, the most formidable organic chemist in Germany let one metaphor escape: to explain why an enzyme would tear apart one molecule and ignore its near-twin, enzyme and substrate had to fit "like lock and key."

scenes.tts: He distrusted the picture even as he offered it — warning it could only be confirmed once someone could isolate a pure enzyme and see its shape.
scenes.visual: distrust; pure enzyme isolated, shape seen
scenes.narration: He distrusted the picture even as he offered it — warning it could only be confirmed once someone could isolate a pure enzyme and see its shape.

scenes.tts: He was right; it took most of a century, and the crystallographers who finally arrived found enzymes don't sit rigid like a brass lock but flex and close around what they bind — the "induced fit" correction Koshland would later make.
scenes.visual: most of a century; rigid lock vs flexing enzyme; induced fit

scenes.tts: Fischer reached the idea the way he cracked the sugars: read the structure off the behavior. He had caged the invisible geometry of glucose with melting points and degradation products, built sugars from glycerol to prove life holds no chemistry beyond the ordinary, named the peptide bond, and trained a generation of Nobel laureates.

scenes.tts: The phenylhydrazine that fingerprinted his sugars also, slowly, poisoned him. He died in 1919.
